newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists push for change of tack on Europe.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists push for change of tack on Europe.

text.p: France's main opposition Socialist party would refuse to back monetary union if it could not get EU governments to consider giving it a more political dimension, the party's European specialist said on Wednesday.
This would include a European economic government, he said.

The Socialists, campaigning for parliamentary elections on May 25 and June 1, also want to reopen talks on the European Union's budget stability pact and get a flexible interpretation of Maastricht treaty criteria for joining a single currency.
Henri Nallet, a former justice minister, said the crucial issue was to get a political debate going in Europe which would make monetary union more meaningful to ordinary people.

"If we have to live through a moment of high tension, and insist our demands are taken into consideration, we will do it. That is the view of (Socialist leader Lionel) Jospin," he told Reuters in an interview.
"We do not want to silence our demands purely in the name of European integration," he said.

The Socialist approach contrasts starkly with that of the governing centre-right coalition, which has kept deliberately quiet recently over how it wants monetary union to evolve to avoid exacerbating German fears about abandoning their mark.

Nallet said the Socialists were open to debate on its conditions and would not insist on them being met to the letter -- "for example the economic government might not be up and running, but we would have made a decision in this direction."
"It will not be because one or other condition is not completely met that we would not give our agreement," he said.

"It is clear however when we say we must have as many countries as possible in the single currency, there must be an economic government, there must be a solidarity pact -- in other words a commitment for Europe to redirect its economic policies to creating jobs.
"If none of that is taken into consideration, this Europe does not interest us very much and indeed we will not give our agreement," he added.
He accused the government of abandoning too quickly French calls for a European economic government, dismissing its toned-down plans for an EU "stability council" as cosmetic.
"We want this question looked at again."
The stability pact, which will impose fines on countries if their deficits overshoot three percent of gross domestic product, would have to be "revisited and completed".
"We must try to put the stability pact back on the negotiating table," he said.

"If it remains as it is, we do not want this stability pact. We have to add something -- the contents of an economic policy," he said. "This exclusively numerical vision is not enough. We will first of all question the figures."

He declined to say exactly what the Socialist party meant when it called for a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht treaty, though he said political talk on whether deficits should be 3.0 percent of GDP or 3.1 percent was wrong.
Socialist Party leader Jospin has said a government under his leadership would not impose a new round of austerity just to bring the deficit to exactly three percent of GDP.
"Obviously the figures cannot be too far away for the average index on the convergence criteria," Nallet said.
But it was impossible for the party to comment definitively on the deficit as it did not have access to the figures. Its first act would be to carry out an audit of public finances.
